e-9460.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over an Ellipse
e-9460.problem: What expression is equivalent to $\displaystyle \int_\limits{C} \dfrac{x}{y} \: \textrm{d}s,$ where $C$ is the ellipse $x^2 + 16y^2 = 16,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?
e-9460.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{4^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{1^2} = 1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $4$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle 4\cos{t}, \: \sin{t} \right\rangle, \qquad 0 \le t \lt 2\pi.
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = \dfrac{x}{y},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{4\operatorname{cos}⁡t}{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}=4\operatorname{cot}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{x}{y}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\operatorname{cot}⁡t\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cot}⁡t\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

e-9488.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over a Part-Ellipse
e-9488.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057969/assets/71df4fc7bd52fe5dd97c7e01502dec2ad68ae31fdf224cccd812c6b7318c70b7.png)

Find, as a definite integral, an expression for the line integral of the function $\displaystyle\int_\limits{C} 2xy \:\textrm{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the right half of the ellipse $9x^2 + 4y^2 = 36,$ shown above.
e-9488.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\dfrac{x^2}{2^2} + \dfrac{y^2}{3^2} = 1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $3,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \left\langle 2\cos{t}, \: 3\sin{t} \right\rangle, \qquad -\dfrac{\pi}{2} \le t \le \dfrac{\pi}{2}.
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+4}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = 2xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =12\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}12\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+4}\,\text{d}t \\  & =12{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{5{cos}^{2}⁡t+4}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

e-9439.knowledge_point: Computing a Line Integral of a Function Over an Ellipse
e-9439.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057969/assets/fda8bfb0533b86dc4050d1b8e309e332996b26263b1052d3e251bf0a5c98e816.png)

Evaluate the line integral $\displaystyle\int_\limits{C}12xy\:\textrm{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the quarter-ellipse $4x^2+y^2=4$ traversed from the point $(0,2)$ to the point $(-1,0),$ as shown above.
e-9439.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
\int\limits_C f(x, y) \, \textrm{d}s  = \int\limits_a^b  f(\mathbf r(t)) \, \| \mathbf r'(t) \| \, \textrm{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
x^2 + \dfrac{y^2}{2^2}  = 1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $2,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
\mathbf{r}(t) = \big\langle \cos{t}, \: 2\sin{t} \big\rangle, \qquad \dfrac{\pi}{2} \le t \le \pi.
$$

Computing $\mathbf{r}'(t)$ and $\| \mathbf{r}'(t) \|,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{3{cos}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{1+3{cos}^{2}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y) = 12xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =12\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t=24\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}12xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }24\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{1+3{cos}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =24{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{1+3{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+3\cos^2 {t},$ $\textrm d u=-6\sin t\cos 
 t\,\textrm d t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}24{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{1+3{cos}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & =-4{\int }_{1}^{4}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =-4\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{1}^{4} \\  & =-\frac{8}{3}({4}^{3/2}-{1}^{3/2}) \\  & =-\frac{8}{3}(8-1) \\  & =-\frac{56}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 1
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x2−8y2)ds, where C is the ellipse x2+8y2=8, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?

a
 4∫02πsin⁡2t7sin2⁡t+1dt
b
8∫02πcos⁡2t3sin2⁡t+4dt
c
 8∫02πsin⁡2t3sin2⁡t+4dt
d
8∫02πcos⁡2t7sin2⁡t+1dt
e
4∫02πcos⁡2tsin2⁡t+7dt
Submit

decision.explanation: Parametrize the ellipse counterclockwise by r(t) = (√8 cos(t), sin(t)), 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π. Then x² − 8y² = 8cos(2t), and ds = √(8sin²(t) + cos²(t)) dt = √(7sin²(t) + 1) dt. Substitution gives option d.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-8{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the ellipse ${x}^{2}+8{y}^{2}=8,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{(2\sqrt{2})^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2\sqrt{2}$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{8{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{7{sin}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{7{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-8{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}-8(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =8{cos}^{2}⁡t-8{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =8({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-8{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\sqrt{7{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\sqrt{7{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 1
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(x2−8y2)ds, where C is the ellipse x2+8y2=8, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?

a
 4∫02πsin⁡2t7sin2⁡t+1dt
b
8∫02πcos⁡2t3sin2⁡t+4dt
c
 8∫02πsin⁡2t3sin2⁡t+4dt
d
8∫02πcos⁡2t7sin2⁡t+1dt
e
4∫02πcos⁡2tsin2⁡t+7dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form x2(22)2+y212=1.

So, the curve C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 22 and 1, respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as r(t)=⟨22cos⁡t,sin⁡t⟩,0≤t<2π.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get following: r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(22cos⁡t)i+ddt(sin⁡t)j=−22sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−22sin⁡t)2+(cos⁡t)2=8sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t=7sin2⁡t+(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=7sin2⁡t+1

Now, since f(x,y)=x2−8y2, we obtain f(r(t))=(22cos⁡t)2−8(sin⁡t)2=8cos2⁡t−8sin2⁡t=8(cos2⁡t−sin2⁡t)=8cos⁡2t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫C(x2−8y2)ds=∫02πf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫02π8cos⁡2t7sin2⁡t+1dt=8∫02πcos⁡2t7sin2⁡t+1dt.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over an Ellipse
content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-8{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the ellipse ${x}^{2}+8{y}^{2}=8,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{(2\sqrt{2})^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2\sqrt{2}$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{8{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{7{sin}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{7{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}-8{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}-8(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =8{cos}^{2}⁡t-8{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =8({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}({x}^{2}-8{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\sqrt{7{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =8{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡2t\sqrt{7{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C2xds, where C is the ellipse 4x2+16y2=64, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?

a
4∫02πcos⁡t3sin2⁡t+1dt
b
16∫02πsin⁡t3sin2⁡t+1dt
c
8∫02πsin⁡tsin2⁡t+3dt
d
8∫02πcos⁡tsin2⁡t+3dt
e
16∫02πcos⁡t3sin2⁡t+1dt
Submit

decision.explanation: The ellipse has parametrization r(t) = (4cos(t), 2sin(t)), 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π, traversed counterclockwise. Thus 2x = 8cos(t) and ds = 2√(3sin²(t)+1) dt, giving option e directly. All displayed integrals also equal zero by cancellation under t → t+π, so they are numerically equivalent; e is the direct parametrized expression.

after.name: Question 2
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}2x\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the ellipse $4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=64,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $4$ and $2,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{12{sin}^{2}⁡t+4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{12{sin}^{2}⁡t+4} \\  & =2\sqrt{3{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=8\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2x\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 2\sqrt{3{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{3{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 2
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C2xds, where C is the ellipse 4x2+16y2=64, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?

a
4∫02πcos⁡t3sin2⁡t+1dt
b
16∫02πsin⁡t3sin2⁡t+1dt
c
8∫02πsin⁡tsin2⁡t+3dt
d
8∫02πcos⁡tsin2⁡t+3dt
e
16∫02πcos⁡t3sin2⁡t+1dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form x242+y222=1.

So, the curve C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 4 and 2, respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as r(t)=⟨4cos⁡t,2sin⁡t⟩,0≤t<2π.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get following: r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(4cos⁡t)i+ddt(2sin⁡t)j=−4sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−4sin⁡t)2+(2cos⁡t)2=16sin2⁡t+4cos2⁡t=12sin2⁡t+4(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=12sin2⁡t+4=23sin2⁡t+1

Now, since f(x,y)=2x, we obtain f(r(t))=2(4cos⁡t)=8cos⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫C2xds=∫02πf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫02π8cos⁡t⋅23sin2⁡t+1dt=16∫02πcos⁡t3sin2⁡t+1dt.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms e: r(t) = (4cos(t), 2sin(t)) gives 2x = 8cos(t) and ds = 2√(3sin²(t)+1) dt, so their product yields the displayed factor 16. All choices evaluate to zero by cancellation under t → t+π, but e directly matches the parametrization and worked solution. The recorded incorrect submission was deliberately option b, not the previously selected e.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over an Ellipse
content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}2x\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the ellipse $4{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=64,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $4$ and $2,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{12{sin}^{2}⁡t+4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{12{sin}^{2}⁡t+4} \\  & =2\sqrt{3{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2x,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)=8\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2x\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }8\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 2\sqrt{3{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{3{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 3
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C2xyds, where C is the ellipse 8x2+2y2=16, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?

a
2∫02πsin⁡2t6cos2⁡t+2dt
b
4∫02πsin⁡2t6cos2⁡t+2dt
c
4∫02πsin⁡2t2cos2⁡t+4dt
d
2∫02πsin⁡2t2cos2⁡t+4dt
e
∫02πsin⁡2t6cos2⁡t+2dt
Submit

decision.explanation: Parametrize counterclockwise by r(t) = (√2 cos(t), 2√2 sin(t)), 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π. Then 2xy = 8cos(t)sin(t) = 4sin(2t), and ds = √(2sin²(t)+8cos²(t)) dt = √(6cos²(t)+2) dt. This gives b directly. All displayed integrals also equal zero by reflection symmetry, so they are numerically equivalent; b matches the direct substitution.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}2xy\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the ellipse $8{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}=16,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{(2\sqrt{2})^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $\sqrt{2}$ and $2\sqrt{2},$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2{sin}^{2}⁡t+8{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{6{cos}^{2}⁡t+2({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{6{cos}^{2}⁡t+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =4\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\sqrt{6{cos}^{2}⁡t+2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\sqrt{6{cos}^{2}⁡t+2}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 3
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C2xyds, where C is the ellipse 8x2+2y2=16, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?

a
2∫02πsin⁡2t6cos2⁡t+2dt
b
4∫02πsin⁡2t6cos2⁡t+2dt
c
4∫02πsin⁡2t2cos2⁡t+4dt
d
2∫02πsin⁡2t2cos2⁡t+4dt
e
∫02πsin⁡2t6cos2⁡t+2dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form x2(2)2+y2(22)2=1.

So, the curve C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 2 and 22, respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as r(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,22sin⁡t⟩,0≤t<2π.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get following: r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(2cos⁡t)i+ddt(22sin⁡t)j=−2sin⁡ti+22cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−2sin⁡t)2+(22cos⁡t)2=2sin2⁡t+8cos2⁡t=6cos2⁡t+2(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=6cos2⁡t+2

Now, since f(x,y)=2xy, we obtain f(r(t))=2(2cos⁡t)(22sin⁡t)=8sin⁡tcos⁡t=4⋅2sin⁡tcos⁡t=4sin⁡2t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫C2xyds=∫02πf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫02π4sin⁡2t6cos2⁡t+2dt=4∫02πsin⁡2t6cos2⁡t+2dt.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over an Ellipse
content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}2xy\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the ellipse $8{x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}=16,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{(2\sqrt{2})^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $\sqrt{2}$ and $2\sqrt{2},$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{2{sin}^{2}⁡t+8{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{6{cos}^{2}⁡t+2({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{6{cos}^{2}⁡t+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=2xy,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =2(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(2\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =4\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t \\  & =4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}2xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }4\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\sqrt{6{cos}^{2}⁡t+2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡2t\sqrt{6{cos}^{2}⁡t+2}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 4
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(3−x2)ds, where C is the ellipse 12x2+3y2=36, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?

a
3∫02πsin2⁡t6cos2⁡t+4dt
b
3∫02πsin2⁡t9cos2⁡t+3dt
c
3∫02πcos2⁡t9cos2⁡t+3dt
d
∫02πsin2⁡t6cos2⁡t+4dt
e
 ∫02πcos2⁡t3cos2⁡t+9dt
Submit

decision.explanation: Write the ellipse as x²/3 + y²/12 = 1 and parametrize counterclockwise by r(t) = (√3 cos(t), 2√3 sin(t)), 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π. Then 3−x² = 3sin²(t), while ds = √(3sin²(t)+12cos²(t)) dt = √(9cos²(t)+3) dt. Substitution gives option b.

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(3-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the ellipse $12{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}=36,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{(2\sqrt{3})^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $\sqrt{3}$ and $2\sqrt{3},$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3{sin}^{2}⁡t+12{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t+3({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t+3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=3-{x}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3-(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =3-3{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =3(1-{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =3{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(3-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3{sin}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t+3}\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t+3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 4
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C(3−x2)ds, where C is the ellipse 12x2+3y2=36, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?

a
3∫02πsin2⁡t6cos2⁡t+4dt
b
3∫02πsin2⁡t9cos2⁡t+3dt
c
3∫02πcos2⁡t9cos2⁡t+3dt
d
∫02πsin2⁡t6cos2⁡t+4dt
e
 ∫02πcos2⁡t3cos2⁡t+9dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form x2(3)2+y2(23)2=1.

So, the curve C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 3 and 23, respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as r(t)=⟨3cos⁡t,23sin⁡t⟩,0≤t<2π.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get following: r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(3cos⁡t)i+ddt(23sin⁡t)j=−3sin⁡ti+23cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−3sin⁡t)2+(23cos⁡t)2=3sin2⁡t+12cos2⁡t=9cos2⁡t+3(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=9cos2⁡t+3

Now, since f(x,y)=3−x2, we obtain f(r(t))=3−(3cos⁡t)2=3−3cos2⁡t=3(1−cos2⁡t)=3sin2⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫C(3−x2)ds=∫02πf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫02π3sin2⁡t9cos2⁡t+3dt=3∫02πsin2⁡t9cos2⁡t+3dt.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms b. With r(t) = (√3 cos(t), 2√3 sin(t)), we obtain 3−x² = 3sin²(t) and ds = √(9cos²(t)+3) dt. Their product gives exactly option b. The recorded incorrect submission was deliberately option e; it does not contradict the earlier answer b.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over an Ellipse
content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}(3-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the ellipse $12{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}=36,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{(2\sqrt{3})^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $\sqrt{3}$ and $2\sqrt{3},$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3{sin}^{2}⁡t+12{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t+3({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t+3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=3-{x}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3-(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =3-3{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =3(1-{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =3{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(3-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3{sin}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t+3}\,\text{d}t \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{9{cos}^{2}⁡t+3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 5
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C3yds, where C is the ellipse 49x2+y2=49, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?

a
3∫02πsin⁡t48cos2⁡t+1dt
b
3∫02πcos⁡tcos2⁡t+48dt
c
21∫02πsin⁡t48cos2⁡t+1dt
d
21∫02πsin⁡tcos2⁡t+48dt
e
21∫02πcos⁡t48cos2⁡t+1dt
Submit

decision.explanation: Parametrize counterclockwise by r(t) = (cos(t), 7sin(t)), 0 ≤ t ≤ 2π. Then 3y = 21sin(t) and ds = √(sin²(t)+49cos²(t)) dt = √(48cos²(t)+1) dt, giving option c. All displayed integrals also equal zero by cancellation under t → t+π; c is the direct parametrized expression.

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}3y\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the ellipse $49{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=49,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{7}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $7,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,7\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(7\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+7\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(7\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+49{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{48{cos}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{48{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=3y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3(7\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=21\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}3y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }21\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{48{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =21{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{48{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Which of the following is equivalent to ∫C3yds, where C is the ellipse 49x2+y2=49, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?

a
3∫02πsin⁡t48cos2⁡t+1dt
b
3∫02πcos⁡tcos2⁡t+48dt
c
21∫02πsin⁡t48cos2⁡t+1dt
d
21∫02πsin⁡tcos2⁡t+48dt
e
21∫02πcos⁡t48cos2⁡t+1dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form x212+y272=1.

So, the curve C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 1 and 7, respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as r(t)=⟨cos⁡t,7sin⁡t⟩,0≤t<2π.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get following: r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(cos⁡t)i+ddt(7sin⁡t)j=−sin⁡ti+7cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−sin⁡t)2+(7cos⁡t)2=sin2⁡t+49cos2⁡t=48cos2⁡t+(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=48cos2⁡t+1

Now, since f(x,y)=3y, we obtain f(r(t))=3(7sin⁡t)=21sin⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫C3yds=∫02πf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫02π21sin⁡t48cos2⁡t+1dt=21∫02πsin⁡t48cos2⁡t+1dt.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over an Ellipse
content.problem: Which of the following is equivalent to ${\int }_{C}3y\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the ellipse $49{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=49,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction?
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{7}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $7,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,7\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t<2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(7\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+7\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(7\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+49{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{48{cos}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{48{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=3y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3(7\operatorname{sin}⁡t)=21\operatorname{sin}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}3y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }21\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{48{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =21{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\sqrt{48{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Which of the following gives the line integral ∫Cx2yds, where the curve C is the quarter of the ellipse 4x2+3y2=12, located in the second quadrant, shown above?

a
6∫0πsin⁡tcos2⁡tcos2⁡t+3dt
b
6∫π/2πsin⁡tcos2⁡t3cos2⁡t+1dt
c
6∫π/2πsin⁡tcos2⁡tcos2⁡t+3dt
d
23∫π/2πsin2⁡t3cos2⁡t+1dt
e
23∫0πsin2⁡tcos2⁡t+3dt
Submit

decision.explanation: Parametrize the second-quadrant arc by r(t) = (√3 cos(t), 2sin(t)), π/2 ≤ t ≤ π, matching the arrows. Then x²y = 6sin(t)cos²(t) and ds = √(3sin²(t)+4cos²(t)) dt = √(cos²(t)+3) dt. Substitution gives option c.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057969/assets/7fc64a261de4941b5ad35b8308b82b0f51c6b6bfbde177aafd793a0a0ac99da6.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the quarter of the ellipse $4{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}=12,$ located in the second quadrant, shown above?
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $\sqrt{3}$ and $2,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+3({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =3{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }6\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+3}\,\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 6
?

Which of the following gives the line integral ∫Cx2yds, where the curve C is the quarter of the ellipse 4x2+3y2=12, located in the second quadrant, shown above?

a
6∫0πsin⁡tcos2⁡tcos2⁡t+3dt
b
6∫π/2πsin⁡tcos2⁡t3cos2⁡t+1dt
c
6∫π/2πsin⁡tcos2⁡tcos2⁡t+3dt
d
23∫π/2πsin2⁡t3cos2⁡t+1dt
e
23∫0πsin2⁡tcos2⁡t+3dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form x2(3)2+y222=1.

So, the curve C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 3 and 2, respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as r(t)=⟨3cos⁡t,2sin⁡t⟩,π2≤t≤π.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get following: r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(3cos⁡t)i+ddt(2sin⁡t)j=−3sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−3sin⁡t)2+(2cos⁡t)2=3sin2⁡t+4cos2⁡t=cos2⁡t+3(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=cos2⁡t+3

Now, since f(x,y)=x2y, we obtain f(r(t))=(3cos⁡t)2(2sin⁡t)=3cos2⁡t⋅2sin⁡t=6sin⁡tcos2⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫Cx2yds=∫π/2πf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫π/2π6sin⁡tcos2⁡tcos2⁡t+3dt=6∫π/2πsin⁡tcos2⁡tcos2⁡t+3dt.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms c. For r(t) = (√3 cos(t), 2sin(t)), π/2 ≤ t ≤ π, we have x²y = 6sin(t)cos²(t) and ds = √(cos²(t)+3) dt. Their product gives option c. The recorded incorrect submission was deliberately d, not the earlier answer c.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over a Part-Ellipse
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057969/assets/7fc64a261de4941b5ad35b8308b82b0f51c6b6bfbde177aafd793a0a0ac99da6.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral ${\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the quarter of the ellipse $4{x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}=12,$ located in the second quadrant, shown above?
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $\sqrt{3}$ and $2,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,2\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{3{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+3({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+3}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)={x}^{2}y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =3{cos}^{2}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =6\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }6\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+3}\,\text{d}t \\  & =6{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t{cos}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{{cos}^{2}⁡t+3}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 7
?

Which of the following gives the line integral ∫C4yxds, where the curve C is the left half of the ellipse x2+16y2=16, shown above?

a
∫π/23π/2cot⁡t5sin2⁡t+3dt
b
∫π/23π/24tan⁡t5sin2⁡t+3dt
c
∫−π/2π/2tan⁡t15sin2⁡t+1dt
d
∫π/23π/2tan⁡t15sin2⁡t+1dt
e
∫−π/2π/24cot⁡tsin2⁡t+15dt
Submit

decision.explanation: Parametrize the shown left half by r(t) = (4cos(t), sin(t)), π/2 ≤ t ≤ 3π/2. Then 4y/x = tan(t) and ds = √(16sin²(t)+cos²(t)) dt = √(15sin²(t)+1) dt, giving d. The integrand is singular at both endpoints, so this is an improper integral that does not converge to a finite value; d correctly expresses it.

after.name: Question 7
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057969/assets/3bf746cfb21805587a65c7beeac90e75464f630bab1fbf3453de69ca3e6639eb.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral ${\int }_{C}\frac{4y}{x}\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the left half of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=16,$ shown above?
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $4$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{4y}{x},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{4y}{x} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{4y}{x}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{tan}⁡t\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 7
?

Which of the following gives the line integral ∫C4yxds, where the curve C is the left half of the ellipse x2+16y2=16, shown above?

a
∫π/23π/2cot⁡t5sin2⁡t+3dt
b
∫π/23π/24tan⁡t5sin2⁡t+3dt
c
∫−π/2π/2tan⁡t15sin2⁡t+1dt
d
∫π/23π/2tan⁡t15sin2⁡t+1dt
e
∫−π/2π/24cot⁡tsin2⁡t+15dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

x242+y2=1.

So, the curve C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 4 and 1, respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨4cos⁡t,sin⁡t⟩,π2≤t≤3π2.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get following:

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(4cos⁡t)i+ddt(sin⁡t)j=−4sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−4sin⁡t)2+(cos⁡t)2=16sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t=15sin2⁡t+(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=15sin2⁡t+1

Now, since f(x,y)=4yx, we obtain

f(r(t))=4yx=4⋅sin⁡t(4cos⁡t)=tan⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as

∫C4yxds=∫π/23π/2f(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫π/23π/2tan⁡t15sin2⁡t+1dt.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over a Part-Ellipse
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057969/assets/3bf746cfb21805587a65c7beeac90e75464f630bab1fbf3453de69ca3e6639eb.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral ${\int }_{C}\frac{4y}{x}\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the left half of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=16,$ shown above?
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $4$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{4y}{x},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{4y}{x} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{4y}{x}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{tan}⁡t\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{4y}{x} \\  & =4\cdot \frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)} \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{4y}{x}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{tan}⁡t\sqrt{15{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

x242+y2=1.

So, the curve C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 4 and 1, respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨4cos⁡t,sin⁡t⟩,π2≤t≤3π2.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get following:

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(4cos⁡t)i+ddt(sin⁡t)j=−4sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−4sin⁡t)2+(cos⁡t)2=16sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t=15sin2⁡t+(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=15sin2⁡t+1

Now, since f(x,y)=4yx, we obtain

f(r(t))=4yx=4⋅sin⁡t(4cos⁡t)=tan⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as

∫C4yxds=∫π/23π/2f(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫π/23π/2tan⁡t15sin2⁡t+1dt.

Question 8
?

Which of the following gives the line integral ∫C(25−x2)ds, where the curve C is three-quarters of the ellipse 36x2+25y2=900, shown above?

a
25∫π/22πcos2⁡t11cos2⁡t+25dt
b
25∫π/22πsin2⁡t11cos2⁡t+25dt
c
36∫π/22πcos2⁡t36cos2⁡t+11dt
d
36∫03π/2cos2⁡t11cos2⁡t+25dt
e
25∫03π/2sin2⁡t36cos2⁡t+11dt
Submit

decision.explanation: Parametrize the shown arc by r(t) = (5cos(t), 6sin(t)), π/2 ≤ t ≤ 2π. Then 25−x² = 25sin²(t), and ds = √(25sin²(t)+36cos²(t)) dt = √(11cos²(t)+25) dt. Substitution gives option b.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057969/assets/34b4b349b8295ee6443a85f019f6bf5e7ea6c6aafe9109ac7935610e6aefcacf.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral ${\int }_{C}(25-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is three-quarters of the ellipse $36{x}^{2}+25{y}^{2}=900,$ shown above?
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{6}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $5$ and $6,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25{sin}^{2}⁡t+36{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{11{cos}^{2}⁡t+25({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{11{cos}^{2}⁡t+25}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=25-{x}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =25-(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =25-25{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =25(1-{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =25{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(25-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }25{sin}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{11{cos}^{2}⁡t+25}\,\text{d}t \\  & =25{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{11{cos}^{2}⁡t+25}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 8
?

Which of the following gives the line integral ∫C(25−x2)ds, where the curve C is three-quarters of the ellipse 36x2+25y2=900, shown above?

a
25∫π/22πcos2⁡t11cos2⁡t+25dt
b
25∫π/22πsin2⁡t11cos2⁡t+25dt
c
36∫π/22πcos2⁡t36cos2⁡t+11dt
d
36∫03π/2cos2⁡t11cos2⁡t+25dt
e
25∫03π/2sin2⁡t36cos2⁡t+11dt
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form x252+y262=1.

So, the curve C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 5 and 6, respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as r(t)=⟨5cos⁡t,6sin⁡t⟩,π2≤t≤2π.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get following: r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(5cos⁡t)i+ddt(6sin⁡t)j=−5sin⁡ti+6cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−5sin⁡t)2+(6cos⁡t)2=25sin2⁡t+36cos2⁡t=11cos2⁡t+25(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=11cos2⁡t+25

Now, since f(x,y)=25−x2, we obtain f(r(t))=25−(5cos⁡t)2=25−25cos2⁡t=25(1−cos2⁡t)=25sin2⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫C(25−x2)ds=∫π/22πf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫π/22π25sin2⁡t11cos2⁡t+25dt=25∫π/22πsin2⁡t11cos2⁡t+25dt.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms b. Parametrizing by r(t) = (5cos(t), 6sin(t)), π/2 ≤ t ≤ 2π, gives 25−x² = 25sin²(t) and ds = √(11cos²(t)+25) dt. Their product matches b exactly. The recorded incorrect submission was deliberately c, not the earlier answer b.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over a Part-Ellipse
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057969/assets/34b4b349b8295ee6443a85f019f6bf5e7ea6c6aafe9109ac7935610e6aefcacf.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral ${\int }_{C}(25-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is three-quarters of the ellipse $36{x}^{2}+25{y}^{2}=900,$ shown above?
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{5}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{6}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $5$ and $6,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨5\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,6\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+6\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-5\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(6\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{25{sin}^{2}⁡t+36{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{11{cos}^{2}⁡t+25({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{11{cos}^{2}⁡t+25}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=25-{x}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =25-(5\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =25-25{cos}^{2}⁡t \\  & =25(1-{cos}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =25{sin}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(25-{x}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }25{sin}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{11{cos}^{2}⁡t+25}\,\text{d}t \\  & =25{\int }_{\pi /2}^{2\pi }{sin}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{11{cos}^{2}⁡t+25}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 9
?

Which of the following gives the line integral ∫Cy2xds, where the curve C is three-quarters of the ellipse 2x2+18y2=36, shown above?

a
12∫03π/2cot⁡t2sin2⁡t+16dt
b
16∫−ππ/2cot⁡t16sin2⁡t+2dt
c
16∫03π/2tan⁡t16sin2⁡t+2dt
d
16∫−ππ/2tan⁡t16sin2⁡t+2dt
e
12∫−ππ/2tan⁡t2sin2⁡t+16dt
Submit

decision.explanation: Parametrize the shown arc by r(t) = (3√2 cos(t), √2 sin(t)), −π ≤ t ≤ π/2, following the arrows. Then y/(2x) = tan(t)/6 and ds = √(18sin²(t)+2cos²(t)) dt = √(16sin²(t)+2) dt, giving d. This expression is improper and does not converge because x vanishes along the arc.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057969/assets/59296f25e2060b05f95ddc69f560e987f933d69f8966c1859ea0cd54bbb80175.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral ${\int }_{C}\frac{y}{2x}\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is three-quarters of the ellipse $2{x}^{2}+18{y}^{2}=36,$ shown above?
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{(3\sqrt{2})^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $3\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{2},$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,-\pi \le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{18{sin}^{2}⁡t+2{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+2({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{y}{2x},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{2(3\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{tan}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{y}{2x}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{tan}⁡t\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi /2}\operatorname{tan}⁡t\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+2}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Which of the following gives the line integral ∫Cy2xds, where the curve C is three-quarters of the ellipse 2x2+18y2=36, shown above?

a
12∫03π/2cot⁡t2sin2⁡t+16dt
b
16∫−ππ/2cot⁡t16sin2⁡t+2dt
c
16∫03π/2tan⁡t16sin2⁡t+2dt
d
16∫−ππ/2tan⁡t16sin2⁡t+2dt
e
12∫−ππ/2tan⁡t2sin2⁡t+16dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form x2(32)2+y2(2)2=1.

So, the curve C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 32 and 2, respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as r(t)=⟨32cos⁡t,2sin⁡t⟩,−π≤t≤π2.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get following: r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(32cos⁡t)i+ddt(2sin⁡t)j=−32sin⁡ti+2cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−32sin⁡t)2+(2cos⁡t)2=18sin2⁡t+2cos2⁡t=16sin2⁡t+2(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=16sin2⁡t+2

Now, since f(x,y)=y2x, we obtain f(r(t))=2sin⁡t2(32cos⁡t)=16tan⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫Cy2xds=∫−ππ/2f(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫−ππ/216tan⁡t16sin2⁡t+2dt=16∫−ππ/2tan⁡t16sin2⁡t+2dt.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over a Part-Ellipse
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057969/assets/59296f25e2060b05f95ddc69f560e987f933d69f8966c1859ea0cd54bbb80175.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral ${\int }_{C}\frac{y}{2x}\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is three-quarters of the ellipse $2{x}^{2}+18{y}^{2}=36,$ shown above?
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{(3\sqrt{2})^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $3\sqrt{2}$ and $\sqrt{2},$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,-\pi \le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{18{sin}^{2}⁡t+2{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+2({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+2}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=\frac{y}{2x},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =\frac{\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t}{2(3\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)} \\  & =\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{tan}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{y}{2x}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi /2}\frac{1}{6}\operatorname{tan}⁡t\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+2}\,\text{d}t \\  & =\frac{1}{6}{\int }_{-\pi }^{\pi /2}\operatorname{tan}⁡t\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+2}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 10
?

Which of the following gives the line integral ∫C(5−y2)ds, where the curve C is three-quarters of the ellipse 5x2+y2=5, shown above?

a
5∫0πsin2⁡t4cos2⁡t+1dt
b
5∫03π/2cos2⁡t4cos2⁡t+1dt
c
∫03π/2cos2⁡tcos2⁡t+4dt
d
5∫03π/2sin2⁡tcos2⁡t+4dt
e
∫0πcos2⁡tcos2⁡t+4dt
Submit

decision.explanation: Parametrize the shown arc by r(t) = (cos(t), √5 sin(t)), 0 ≤ t ≤ 3π/2. Then 5−y² = 5cos²(t), and ds = √(sin²(t)+5cos²(t)) dt = √(4cos²(t)+1) dt. Substitution gives option b.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057969/assets/1e09fa361aca812f22d9d28430a8584e069c0eb9a2aa90f5e665d892dddd378f.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral ${\int }_{C}(5-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is three-quarters of the ellipse $5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=5,$ shown above?
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{(\sqrt{5})^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $\sqrt{5},$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+5{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=5-{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =5-(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =5-5{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =5(1-{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =5{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(5-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}5{cos}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 10
?

Which of the following gives the line integral ∫C(5−y2)ds, where the curve C is three-quarters of the ellipse 5x2+y2=5, shown above?

a
5∫0πsin2⁡t4cos2⁡t+1dt
b
5∫03π/2cos2⁡t4cos2⁡t+1dt
c
∫03π/2cos2⁡tcos2⁡t+4dt
d
5∫03π/2sin2⁡tcos2⁡t+4dt
e
∫0πcos2⁡tcos2⁡t+4dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form x212+y2(5)2=1.

So, the curve C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 1 and 5, respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as r(t)=⟨cos⁡t,5sin⁡t⟩,0≤t≤3π2.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get following: r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(cos⁡t)i+ddt(5sin⁡t)j=−sin⁡ti+5cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−sin⁡t)2+(5cos⁡t)2=sin2⁡t+5cos2⁡t=4cos2⁡t+(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=4cos2⁡t+1

Now, since f(x,y)=5−y2, we obtain f(r(t))=5−(5sin⁡t)2=5−5sin2⁡t=5(1−sin2⁡t)=5cos2⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫C(5−y2)ds=∫03π/2f(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫03π/25cos2⁡t4cos2⁡t+1dt=5∫03π/2cos2⁡t4cos2⁡t+1dt.

content.knowledge_point: Constructing the Line Integral of a Function Over a Part-Ellipse
content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057969/assets/1e09fa361aca812f22d9d28430a8584e069c0eb9a2aa90f5e665d892dddd378f.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral ${\int }_{C}(5-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is three-quarters of the ellipse $5{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=5,$ shown above?
content.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{1}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{(\sqrt{5})^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $1$ and $\sqrt{5},$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \frac{3\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{{sin}^{2}⁡t+5{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=5-{y}^{2},$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =5-(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2} \\  & =5-5{sin}^{2}⁡t \\  & =5(1-{sin}^{2}⁡t) \\  & =5{cos}^{2}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(5-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}5{cos}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =5{\int }_{0}^{3\pi /2}{cos}^{2}⁡t\sqrt{4{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

before.html:
Question 11
?

Evaluate the line integral ∫C16xyds, where the curve C is the quarter of the ellipse x2+9y2=9 traversed from the point (0,1) to the point (−3,0).

a
 56
b
 −48
c
 48
d
 −52
e
 −34
Submit

decision.explanation: Use r(t) = (3cos(t), sin(t)), π/2 ≤ t ≤ π. The integral becomes 48∫ sin(t)cos(t)√(1+8sin²(t)) dt. With u = 1+8sin²(t), du = 16sin(t)cos(t) dt, the bounds are 9 and 1. Thus the value is 3∫₉¹√u du = 2(1−27) = −52, giving d.

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057969/assets/570b00c901daedddc9fe05855e2df5fb2c24158320544b955bda651210d9f803.png)

Evaluate the line integral ${\int }_{C}16xy\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the quarter of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}=9$  traversed from the point $(0,1)$ to the point $(-3,0).$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $3$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{8{sin}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{1+8{sin}^{2}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=16xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =16\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t=48\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}16xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }48\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{1+8{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =48{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{1+8{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+8{sin}^{2}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}48{\int }_{\pi /2}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{1+8{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & =3{\int }_{9}^{1}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =3\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{9}^{1} \\  & =2({1}^{3/2}-{9}^{3/2}) \\  & =2(1-27) \\  & =-52\end{aligned}
$$

after.html:
Question 11
?

Evaluate the line integral ∫C16xyds, where the curve C is the quarter of the ellipse x2+9y2=9 traversed from the point (0,1) to the point (−3,0).

a
 56
b
 −48
c
 48
d
 −52
e
 −34
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

x232+y2=1.

So, the curve C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 3 and 1, respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨3cos⁡t,sin⁡t⟩,π2≤t≤π.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get following:

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(3cos⁡t)i+ddt(sin⁡t)j=−3sin⁡ti+cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−3sin⁡t)2+(cos⁡t)2=9sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t=8sin2⁡t+(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=1+8sin2⁡t

Now, since f(x,y)=16xy, we obtain

f(r(t))=16⋅3cos⁡t⋅sin⁡t=48sin⁡tcos⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as

∫C16xyds=∫π/2πf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫π/2π48sin⁡tcos⁡t⋅1+8sin2⁡t⋅dt=48∫π/2πsin⁡tcos⁡t1+8sin2⁡tdt.

We can solve this using the substitution u=1+8sin2⁡t, du=16sin⁡tcos⁡tdt as follows:

48∫π/2πsin⁡tcos⁡t1+8sin2⁡tdt=3∫91udu=3⋅23u3/2|91=2(13/2−93/2)=2(1−27)=−52

decision.explanation: The ellipse is symmetric under reflection (x,y) → (−x,y). This reflection preserves ds and changes 9xy to −9xy, so contributions from the two halves cancel. Therefore the line integral is 0, option d.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=9xy$ along the ellipse $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+9{y}^{2}=16,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction.
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{(\frac{4}{3})}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $4$ and $\frac{4}{3},$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+{(\frac{4}{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+\frac{16}{9}{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\sqrt{8{sin}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}\sqrt{8{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=9xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =9\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \frac{4}{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t=48\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}9xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }48\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \frac{4}{3}\sqrt{8{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =64{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{8{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=8{sin}^{2}⁡t+1,$ $\text{d}u=16\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}64{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{8{sin}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t & =4{\int }_{1}^{1}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =4\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{1}^{1} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

x242+y2(43)2=1.

So, the curve C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 4 and 43, respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨4cos⁡t,43sin⁡t⟩,0≤t≤2π.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get following:

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(4cos⁡t)i+ddt(43sin⁡t)j=−4sin⁡ti+43cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−4sin⁡t)2+(43cos⁡t)2=16sin2⁡t+169cos2⁡t=439sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t=438sin2⁡t+(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=438sin2⁡t+1

Now, since f(x,y)=9xy, we obtain

f(r(t))=9⋅4cos⁡t⋅43sin⁡t=48sin⁡tcos⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as

∫C9xyds=∫02πf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫02π48sin⁡tcos⁡t⋅438sin2⁡t+1⋅dt=64∫02πsin⁡tcos⁡t8sin2⁡t+1dt.

We can solve this using the substitution u=8sin2⁡t+1, du=16sin⁡tcos⁡tdt as follows:

64∫02πsin⁡tcos⁡t8sin2⁡t+1dt=4∫11udu=4⋅23u3/2|11=0

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms 0, option d. Reflection across the y-axis preserves the ellipse and ds while reversing the sign of 9xy, so the contributions cancel. Equivalently, the parametrized integrand has antiderivative (8/3)(8sin²(t)+1)^(3/2), whose values at 0 and 2π agree. The deliberately incorrect submission was a, not the earlier answer d.

$$

before.html:
Question 13
?

Evaluate the line integral ∫C7xyds, where the curve C is the quarter of the ellipse 9x2+16y2=144 traversed from the point (0,−3) to the point (4,0).

a
 −148
b
 −64
c
 −42
d
 64
e
 84
Submit

decision.explanation: Parametrize by r(t) = (4cos(t), 3sin(t)), −π/2 ≤ t ≤ 0. Then 7xy = 84sin(t)cos(t) and ds = √(9+7sin²(t)) dt. Setting u = 9+7sin²(t), du = 14sin(t)cos(t) dt, gives 6∫₁₆⁹√u du = 4(27−64) = −148. Thus option a is correct.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14057969/assets/f1a234c8ec4ac3e2dcc4c2bfd2232c006179a3ca7597c05afbb4243435eca387.png)

Evaluate the line integral ${\int }_{C}7xy\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the quarter of the ellipse $9{x}^{2}+16{y}^{2}=144$  traversed from the point $(0,-3)$ to the point $(4,0).$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $3$ and $4,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨4\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,3\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,\frac{3\pi }{2}\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{16{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{7{sin}^{2}⁡t+(9{sin}^{2}⁡t+9{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{9+7{sin}^{2}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=7xy$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =7\cdot 4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 3\operatorname{sin}⁡t=84\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}7xy\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }84\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{9+7{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =84{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{9+7{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=9+7{sin}^{2}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=14\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}84{\int }_{3\pi /2}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\sqrt{9+7{sin}^{2}⁡t}\,\text{d}t & =6{\int }_{16}^{9}\sqrt{u}\,\text{d}u \\  & =6\cdot \frac{2}{3}{u}^{3/2}{|}_{16}^{9} \\  & =4({9}^{3/2}-{16}^{3/2}) \\  & =4(27-64) \\  & =-148\end{aligned}
$$

Question 13
?

Evaluate the line integral ∫C7xyds, where the curve C is the quarter of the ellipse 9x2+16y2=144 traversed from the point (0,−3) to the point (4,0).

a
 −148
b
 −64
c
 −42
d
 64
e
 84
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

x242+y232=1.

So, the curve C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 3 and 4, respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨4cos⁡t,3sin⁡t⟩,3π2≤t≤2π.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get following:

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(4cos⁡t)i+ddt(3sin⁡t)j=−4sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−4sin⁡t)2+(3cos⁡t)2=16sin2⁡t+9cos2⁡t=7sin2⁡t+(9sin2⁡t+9cos2⁡t)=9+7sin2⁡t

Now, since f(x,y)=7xy, we obtain

f(r(t))=7⋅4cos⁡t⋅3sin⁡t=84sin⁡tcos⁡t.

Therefore, we can write the integral as

∫C7xyds=∫3π/22πf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫3π/22π84sin⁡tcos⁡t⋅9+7sin2⁡t⋅dt=84∫3π/22πsin⁡tcos⁡t9+7sin2⁡tdt.

We can solve this using the substitution u=9+7sin2⁡t, du=14sin⁡tcos⁡tdt as follows:

84∫3π/22πsin⁡tcos⁡t9+7sin2⁡tdt=6∫169udu=6⋅23u3/2|169=4(93/2−163/2)=4(27−64)=−148
