decision.explanation: Reflection across the y-axis preserves the ellipse and arc length ds, while xy(3+2y²) changes sign. The contributions from the left and right halves therefore cancel, giving 0, option e.

after.name: Question 14
after.problem: Evaluate the line integral of the function $f(x,y)=xy(3+2{y}^{2})$ along the ellipse $C$ with equation ${x}^{2}+3{y}^{2}=9,$ traversed once in the counterclockwise direction.
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{3}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{(\sqrt{3})^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $3$ and $\sqrt{3},$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨3\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le 2\pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(3\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-3\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{9{sin}^{2}⁡t+3{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{6{sin}^{2}⁡t+3({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{3+6{sin}^{2}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=xy(3+2{y}^{2})$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =3\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (3+2(\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2})=3\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,(3+6{sin}^{2}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}xy(3+2{y}^{2})\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }3\sqrt{3}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t(3+6{sin}^{2}⁡t)\cdot \sqrt{3+6{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =3\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t{(3+6{sin}^{2}⁡t)}^{3/2}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=3+6{sin}^{2}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=12\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}3\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t{(3+6{sin}^{2}⁡t)}^{3/2}\,\text{d}t & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}{\int }_{3}^{3}{u}^{3/2}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{4}\cdot \frac{2}{5}{u}^{5/2}{|}_{3}^{3} \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Question 14

Evaluate the line integral of the function f(x,y)=xy(3+2y2) along the ellipse C with equation x2+3y2=9, traversed once in the counterclockwise direction.

a
 14
b
 33
c
 310
d
 34
e
 0
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula

∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

x232+y2(3)2=1.

So, the curve C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 3 and 3, respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as

r(t)=⟨3cos⁡t,3sin⁡t⟩,0≤t≤2π.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get following:

r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(3cos⁡t)i+ddt(3sin⁡t)j=−3sin⁡ti+3cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−3sin⁡t)2+(3cos⁡t)2=9sin2⁡t+3cos2⁡t=6sin2⁡t+3(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=3+6sin2⁡t

Now, since f(x,y)=xy(3+2y2), we obtain

f(r(t))=3cos⁡t⋅3sin⁡t⋅(3+2(3sin⁡t)2)=33sin⁡tcos⁡t(3+6sin2⁡t).

Therefore, we can write the integral as

∫Cxy(3+2y2)ds=∫02πf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫02π33sin⁡tcos⁡t(3+6sin2⁡t)⋅3+6sin2⁡t⋅dt=33∫02πsin⁡tcos⁡t(3+6sin2⁡t)3/2dt.

We can solve this using the substitution u=3+6sin2⁡t, du=12sin⁡tcos⁡tdt as follows:

33∫02πsin⁡tcos⁡t(3+6sin2⁡t)3/2dt=34∫33u3/2du=34⋅25u5/2|33=0

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms option e, 0. Reflection across the y-axis preserves the ellipse and ds while changing the sign of xy(3+2y²), so the contributions cancel. The recorded incorrect submission was deliberately d, not the earlier answer e.

decision.explanation: Parametrize by r(t) = (√5 cos(t), sin(t)), 0 ≤ t ≤ π/2. Then ds = √(1+4sin²(t)) dt, so the integral is 8√5∫₀^{π/2}sin(t)cos(t)(1+4sin²(t)) dt. With u = 1+4sin²(t), this becomes √5∫₁⁵u du = 12√5, option e.

Evaluate the line integral ${\int }_{C}8xy\sqrt{1+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is the quarter of the ellipse ${x}^{2}+5{y}^{2}=5$  traversed from the point $(\sqrt{5},0)$ to the point $(0,1).$
after.worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{(\sqrt{5})^{2}}+{y}^{2}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $\sqrt{5}$ and $1,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,0\le t\le \frac{\pi }{2}.
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{5{sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{1+4{sin}^{2}⁡t}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=8xy\sqrt{1+4{y}^{2}}$, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =8\cdot \sqrt{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{1+4{sin}^{2}⁡t}=8\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\sqrt{1+4{sin}^{2}⁡t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}8xy\sqrt{1+4{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}8\sqrt{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\sqrt{1+4{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \sqrt{1+4{sin}^{2}⁡t}\cdot \text{d}t \\  & =8\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t(1+4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

We can solve this using the substitution $u=1+4{sin}^{2}⁡t,$ $\text{d}u=8\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,\text{d}t$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}8\sqrt{5}{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\operatorname{cos}⁡t(1+4{sin}^{2}⁡t)\,\text{d}t & =\sqrt{5}{\int }_{1}^{5}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\sqrt{5}\cdot \frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}{|}_{1}^{5} \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}({5}^{2}-{1}^{2}) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{5}}{2}(25-1) \\  & =12\sqrt{5}\end{aligned}
$$
